role: Deals, partners and investors, with Elias (Tax)
title: The waterfall: how profit is shared, and why the order decides who wins
summary: A distribution waterfall is the agreed order in which a joint venture's cash is paid out to investors and to the developer. Return of capital, preferred return and promote each sit in that order. The order, not the headline percentages, decides how the money really divides.
body:
A waterfall is a set of buckets that fill in order: investors get their money back first, then a minimum return, and only then does the developer earn a larger share of the profit. Read the order before you read the percentages.

Recall

Q. What is a standstill in an intercreditor agreement?

A. An agreed period during which one lender may not enforce while another party attempts to cure the default.

Q. What is loan-to-cost, and how does it differ from loan-to-value?

A. Loan-to-cost divides the loan by the project's total cost; loan-to-value divides it by appraised value. During construction lenders lean on cost, because value is still a forecast.

Q. What does title insurance protect against?

A. Loss from defects in title that existed at the policy date and were not excepted, such as an undisclosed lien or a forged prior transfer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week the capital stack told you who is paid first between lenders and owners. This week opens up the top of that stack. Once the lenders are paid, the common equity's cash must be split between the investors who supplied most of the money and the developer who supplied most of the work. That split is the developer's main route to wealth beyond fees, and it is also where most partnership disputes begin. Get the waterfall right and you are paid well for good performance. Get it vague and you will spend the good years arguing.

The buckets, in plain English

A distribution waterfall is the clause in a joint venture or partnership agreement that lists, in order, where each dollar of distributable cash goes. A typical simple version has four buckets. First, every partner gets back the capital it contributed. Second, every partner receives a preferred return, a minimum return on that capital, often expressed as a percentage per year. Third, in some deals the developer receives a catch-up, which we study on day five. Fourth, the remaining profit is split, with the developer receiving more than its share of the capital would justify. That extra share is the promote, sometimes called carried interest.

The percentages used below are hypothetical and illustrate commercial practice. They are negotiated deal by deal and are not set by any standard.

Worked example one: a good outcome

A hypothetical joint venture raises 10 million dollars of equity: 9 million from an investor and 1 million from the developer, a 90 to 10 split. After three years the building is sold and, once the loan is repaid, 16 million dollars is left to distribute. The waterfall is: capital back pro rata; then an 8 percent simple annual preferred return pro rata; then everything above is split 80 percent to all partners pro rata and 20 percent to the developer as promote.

  1. Return of capital: 10 million out, 9 to the investor and 1 to the developer. 6 million remains.
  2. Preferred return: 8 percent of 10 million for three years is 2.4 million, paid 2.16 to the investor and 0.24 to the developer. 3.6 million remains.
  3. Split: 20 percent of 3.6 million, which is 0.72 million, goes to the developer as promote. The other 2.88 million is shared 90 to 10, so 2.592 to the investor and 0.288 to the developer.

Totals: the investor receives 13.752 million on 9 invested, a profit of 4.752 million. The developer receives 2.248 million on 1 invested, a profit of 1.248 million. The developer put in 10 percent of the money and took about 21 percent of the profit. That gap is the reward for creating the deal and running it well.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: a weak outcome

Now the same venture sells for less, and only 12 million is left after the loan. Capital back takes 10 million. The preferred return owed is 2.4 million, but only 2 million remains, so it is all paid pro rata, 1.8 to the investor and 0.2 to the developer. Nothing reaches the promote bucket. The developer receives 1.2 million, a profit of 0.2 million, exactly its share. That is the design working. The promote is paid only when the investors have done well first. A waterfall that pays a promote in this weak case is not sharing upside; it is transferring money.

The professional framing: what to read first

Professionals read a waterfall in a set order. Is the preferred return simple or compounding, and is it measured as a percentage per year or as an internal rate of return? Are distributions tested deal to date, so that a promote paid early can be checked against the final result, or bucket by bucket on each distribution? Is there a clawback, a promise by the developer to pay back promote if later results show it was overpaid? And how are fees, such as a development fee, treated: are they paid outside the waterfall, as a cost of the project, or counted against the developer's share? Each of these can move more money than a change in the headline split.

Worked example three: when the clock starts

The preferred return accrues on capital for the time it is outstanding, so the date each dollar is counted from moves money. Take the good outcome again, but suppose the 10 million was not contributed on day one. Half was called at the start and half 18 months later, both partners funding pro rata, and the sale still comes at year three with 16 million to distribute.

  1. Preferred return: 8 percent of 5 million for three years is 1.2 million, plus 8 percent of 5 million for one and a half years, which is 0.6 million. Total 1.8 million, not 2.4 million.
  2. After capital and the preferred return, 16 minus 10 minus 1.8 leaves 4.2 million.
  3. Promote: 20 percent of 4.2 million is 0.84 million. The other 3.36 million is shared 90 to 10, so 0.336 million to the developer.

The developer now receives 1 plus 0.18 plus 0.84 plus 0.336, which is about 2.356 million, a profit of about 1.356 million instead of 1.248 million. Nothing about the building changed; only the definition of when capital starts earning its return. So read the contribution clause beside the waterfall: when capital is called, when it counts, and whether capital returned early, from a refinance for example, stops earning a return from that date.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a waterfall that pays the promote on an interim distribution, such as a refinance, before the deal's final result is known, with no effective way to get it back if the deal later disappoints. The control is to test every distribution against the whole deal to date, to require a clawback, and to back that clawback with something real: an escrow of part of the promote, or a guarantee from the people who receive it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the split, 80 to 20 or 70 to 30, and accepts the definitions as drafted. The definitions of capital, preferred return and distributable cash decide the outcome more than the split does. Read the definitions first, and run both worked examples through the actual clause.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the developer's fee and the developer's promote may be taxed very differently, so the label on each dollar matters; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a clawback is a personal promise to repay, so understand who gives it and how it is secured. Banking: lenders often restrict distributions while loan tests are failing, which stops the waterfall regardless of what it says. Governance: who decides when to distribute, and who calculates the waterfall, should be written down. Estate: a promote interest held personally may pass on death in ways the partnership agreement restricts; read the transfer clauses. Exit: the waterfall is usually calculated at sale, so a partner's buyout price depends on it; agree the method in advance.

Callback

In week 15 we saw that internal rate of return can be flattered by returning cash early. Waterfalls that measure the preferred return as an internal rate of return have exactly that sensitivity: an early refinance distribution raises the measured return and can unlock promote sooner. When a hurdle is stated as an internal rate of return, ask for an equity multiple hurdle beside it.

Recap

The waterfall is an order: capital back, preferred return, sometimes a catch-up, then a split that includes the promote. The promote should appear only when investors have done well, and every early promote needs a clawback with real security behind it.

Next: Ford, with Cole, takes apart a composite failure: the promote that was paid twice.
checklist: Write the waterfall's buckets in order on one page
Confirm whether the preferred return is simple or compounding
Confirm whether hurdles are a rate of return, a multiple, or both
Check whether distributions are tested against the whole deal to date
Read the clawback and what secures it
Find where fees sit: inside or outside the waterfall
Run a good case and a weak case through the actual clause
Run the Six-Lens Check before agreeing the terms
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the waterfall in sixty seconds. It is the order in which a joint venture pays out cash. First, everyone gets their capital back. Second, everyone gets a preferred return, a minimum return on capital. Sometimes the developer then gets a catch-up. Finally, the rest is split, with the developer getting more than its capital share: that extra is the promote. In a hypothetical 10 million dollar venture, 90 percent from an investor and 10 from the developer, a 16 million result pays the developer about 21 percent of the profit. A 12 million result pays it exactly its 10 percent share and no promote, which is the design working. Read the definitions before the split: simple or compounding pref, rate or multiple hurdles, deal-to-date testing, a secured clawback, and where fees sit. A promote paid early without a secured clawback is the biggest risk.
terms: Distribution waterfall — the clause setting out, in order, how a venture's distributable cash is paid to the partners.
Preferred return — a minimum return on contributed capital that must be paid before profits are shared on other terms.
Promote — the share of profit paid to the developer above its share of contributed capital, as a reward for performance.

hostile.q: Your promote starts after an 8 percent preferred return. What stops you taking promote on a refinance and leaving us short at sale?
hostile.a: Every distribution is tested against the whole deal to date, so promote is only paid if capital and the preferred return have been covered on everything distributed so far. There is a clawback at final sale, and it is secured: a share of any promote paid before sale is held in escrow until the deal closes out. I will walk you through the clause with the weak-case numbers.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole (Audit and integrity)
title: The promote that was paid twice: a composite collapse
summary: A composite case in which a developer took promote on a refinance, collected fees the investors did not fully understand, and then sold at a loss. The clawback existed on paper but had nothing behind it. Taken through seven steps, it shows why waterfalls fail in the drafting, not in the market.
body:
This is a composite example. It is built from patterns that recur in joint venture disputes, not from one real company, and every number is hypothetical. Its lesson is simple: a waterfall fails when money leaves before the result is known and nothing secures its return.

Recall

Q. In the worked capital stack, what did the downside case do to the common equity?

A. With income down 10 percent and the capitalisation rate up a point, value fell to 42 million and the common equity was wiped out, while both lenders were repaid in full.

Q. What is debt yield, and why do some lenders prefer it to coverage?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan. It does not depend on the interest rate or amortisation, so it cannot be flattered by cheap or interest-only debt.

Q. What is an easement?

A. A right attached to land that lets someone else use it for a limited purpose, such as access or a utility line, and that usually survives a sale.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you are the developer, you will draft or accept the waterfall. When you are the investor in someone else's deal, you will rely on it. Either way, the failures below are avoidable at signing and almost impossible to fix afterwards. Cole sits beside Ford today because the root of this case is integrity of records and the character of payments, not the market.

Step 1: Timeline

Year 0: a developer and an investor form a joint venture to build a hypothetical rental building. Equity is 20 million, 18 from the investor and 2 from the developer. Year 3: the building is leased up and refinanced; the new loan returns 12 million of cash to the partners, and the developer is paid a promote on that distribution. Year 4: a large competing project opens nearby, rents soften, and a major repair is needed. Year 6: the building is sold, and after repaying the loan the venture distributes far less than expected. The investor ends with a loss. The developer has already received promote and fees. The investor calls on the clawback. The developer's holding company has distributed the promote to its principals and has no assets.

Step 2: Key decisions

First, agreeing a waterfall that calculated promote on each distribution separately rather than on the deal to date. Second, accepting a clawback given by an empty holding company with no guarantee or escrow. Third, agreeing a development fee, an asset management fee and a refinancing fee, each defined in a different schedule, without a single statement of total fees.

Step 3: Assumptions

Both sides assumed the year-three value was permanent. The investor assumed the clawback clause meant money would come back. The developer assumed promote was earned once the refinance came through. Nobody assumed a competing project, although the land beside them was zoned for one.

Step 4: Incentives

The developer was paid earlier and more surely by refinancing than by holding to sale, so its incentive was to refinance as soon as it could. Fees paid on activity, financing fees in particular, rewarded doing transactions rather than creating value. The investor's staff were measured on capital deployed, so they were inclined to accept terms to close.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The investor's counsel flagged that the clawback party had no assets. The flag was noted and not acted on. The refinance appraisal relied on rents above the submarket average. The quarterly reports showed fees in three separate lines, so no one saw the total. And the developer described the refinancing fee in its own accounts in a way that did not match the partnership agreement, which Cole would have spotted at once: when the same payment has two descriptions, one of them is wrong.

Step 6: The point of no return

The point of no return was the year-three promote. Once it was paid out of an entity with no other assets, the investor's protection became a lawsuit against an empty company. Everything afterwards was the market, and the market is allowed to disappoint.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a waterfall that let promote leave the venture before the result was known, combined with a clawback that had nothing behind it. A secondary cause, Cole's point, was opaque fee reporting that hid the developer's total take.

The applied lesson, in numbers

Worked example one. Suppose the year-three promote paid to the developer was a hypothetical 1.5 million. At final sale, the deal-to-date calculation shows the investor never received its capital and preferred return in full, so the developer should have received no promote at all. The clawback says the developer owes 1.5 million back. If, at signing, 50 percent of any interim promote had been required to sit in escrow until final sale, 750,000 dollars would be sitting in an account ready to return. The other half would rest on a guarantee from the principals. That one clause turns a lawsuit into a transfer.

Worked example two, Cole's fee check. Add every fee the developer received: a development fee of 2 percent of a hypothetical 50 million cost, which is 1 million; asset management fees of 150,000 a year for six years, which is 900,000; and a refinancing fee of 1 percent of a 40 million loan, which is 400,000. Total fees: 2.3 million, more than the developer's own 2 million equity. A developer whose fees exceed its equity can do well while its investor loses. That is not automatically wrong, but it must be disclosed and agreed as a total, not discovered line by line.

Worked example three: the deal-to-date test at year three

Run the year-three refinance through a deal-to-date test instead of a separate calculation, and the promote disappears on the spot. Equity was 20 million. A preferred return of a hypothetical 8 percent simple a year for three years adds 4.8 million. So before any promote is due, the partners must have received 24.8 million in total. The refinance distributed 12 million, less than half of that. Under a deal-to-date test, every dollar of the 12 million is treated as return of capital, and no promote is paid at all. Under the separate calculation the venture actually used, the same 12 million could be run through its own small waterfall, and promote leaked out on cash that was really the investor's own money coming home.

That is the whole case in one comparison: the same cash, the same building, two drafting choices, and a 1.5 million difference in who holds the money when the market turns.

How Ford would read the draft

Before signing, read the waterfall with four questions, in this order. Is every promote tested against the whole deal to date? Who gives the clawback, and what do they own today? What part of any interim promote is held back, and where? Where is the single schedule of every fee, in dollars, over the life of the deal? If any answer is "the clause does not say", the draft is not finished. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer experienced in joint venture agreements, and an accountant to run the waterfall model.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is money leaving the venture on a forecast. The control is deal-to-date testing of every promote payment, a clawback backed by escrow and a guarantee, and a single schedule showing total fees in dollars.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the clawback clause and stops. A clawback is only as good as the assets of the party that gives it. Ask who signs it, what they own, and what is held back.

Callback

In week 24 we separated substance from form. A refinancing fee that appears as a profit share in one place and a service fee in another is a form problem that hides a substance question: what was this payment really for? Cole's rule is that every payment to the developer has one name, one schedule and one explanation.

Recap

The waterfall failed in the drafting: promote measured distribution by distribution, an unsecured clawback, and fees scattered across schedules. Each is fixed at signing with a deal-to-date test, an escrowed and guaranteed clawback, and a total-fee schedule.

Rule 38: No promote is paid until investors have their capital and preferred return on the whole deal to date, and every clawback is backed by escrow or a guarantee from someone with assets.

Next: Sage on the money: how hurdles, catch-ups and fees change each partner's return.
checklist: Confirm promote is tested against the whole deal to date
Identify who gives the clawback and what assets stand behind it
Require an escrow of part of any promote paid before final sale
Prepare one schedule showing every developer fee in dollars
Check that each payment has the same description in every document
Compare total developer fees with the developer's own equity
Map any zoned or approved competing supply near the asset
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, a composite case in sixty seconds. A developer and an investor build a rental building. At year three a refinance returns cash and the developer is paid promote on that distribution alone. Rents later soften, and the sale at year six leaves the investor with a loss. The clawback clause says the developer must repay the promote, but the developer's holding company has already passed the money to its owners and has nothing left. Meanwhile fees were spread across three schedules and totalled more than the developer's own equity. The root cause was letting promote leave before the result was known, with an unsecured clawback. The fix happens at signing: test promote against the whole deal to date, escrow part of any early promote, get a guarantee from people with assets, and show total fees on one schedule. Rule 38 says exactly that.
terms: Clawback — a promise by the developer to repay promote that later results show was overpaid.
Deal-to-date test — calculating the waterfall cumulatively on all distributions so far, rather than separately on each distribution.
Escrow — money held by a neutral party under written instructions until a stated condition is met.

hostile.q: If the deal disappoints after a refinance, how do we actually get our promote back from you?
hostile.a: Half of any promote paid before final sale is held in escrow until the deal closes out, so it returns automatically. The other half is covered by a guarantee from the principals personally, not by the general partner entity. Every distribution is tested deal to date, so promote is only paid once your capital and preferred return are covered on everything distributed so far.

rule: Rule 38: No promote is paid until investors have their capital and preferred return on the whole deal to date, and every clawback is backed by escrow or a guarantee from someone with assets.

title: How hurdles, catch-ups and fees change each partner's return
summary: The same building can produce very different returns for the developer and the investor depending on how the preferred return is measured, whether there is a catch-up, and where fees sit. This lesson prices each lever and shows the developer's real share of profit.
body:
A waterfall is a pricing machine. Change the hurdle, add a catch-up or move a fee, and money moves from one partner to the other without the building earning a cent more or less.

Recall

Q. What is a cash sweep?

A. A requirement that surplus cash flow be applied to repay a loan rather than distributed or held in reserve.

Q. What does fixed versus floating rate debt mean for a developer's risk?

A. A fixed rate locks the interest cost; a floating rate moves with a reference rate, so the cost of carry, and coverage, change with the market unless hedged.

Q. What is an encumbrance on title?

A. Any registered or legal interest that limits the owner's use or transfer of land, such as a mortgage, easement, covenant or lien.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you raise equity you are selling a share of the profit. The waterfall is the price list. If you understand which terms are cheap to give and which are expensive, you can offer investors terms that feel generous while protecting your own reward, and you will know when an investor's request costs you far more than it seems.

Lever one: compounding versus simple

A preferred return can be simple, calculated only on the original capital, or compounding, where unpaid preferred return itself earns a return. Worked example: 10 million of capital, 8 percent per year, nothing paid for three years. Simple: 8 percent of 10 million times three years equals 2.4 million. Compounding annually: 10 million times 1.08 times 1.08 times 1.08 equals about 12.597 million, so the accrued preferred return is about 2.597 million. The difference, about 197,000 dollars, comes straight out of the money that would otherwise reach the promote. On a longer hold, or a higher rate, the gap grows quickly.

Lever two: the catch-up

A catch-up is a bucket after the preferred return in which the developer receives all, or most, of the next dollars until it has received an agreed share of total profit. Without one, the developer's promote applies only to profit above the preferred return. With a full catch-up, the developer ends up with its agreed share of all the profit once returns are high enough. Using last lesson's numbers, a 20 percent promote with a full catch-up gives the developer 20 percent of the entire 6 million profit as promote, which is 1.2 million, instead of 20 percent of 3.6 million, which was 0.72 million. The catch-up moved 480,000 dollars to the developer. Investors know this, so a full catch-up is usually traded for something: a higher hurdle, a smaller split, or a larger developer co-investment.

Say that out loud now.

Lever three: rate hurdles versus multiple hurdles

A hurdle stated as an internal rate of return rewards speed. A hurdle stated as an equity multiple, such as 1.5 times the capital returned, rewards total profit. Worked example: a deal returns 1.3 times capital after one year, an internal rate of return near 30 percent, which beats a 15 percent rate hurdle easily, but falls short of a 1.5 times multiple hurdle. A deal that returns 1.8 times after eight years has an internal rate of return of under 8 percent, failing the rate hurdle but clearing the multiple. Investors increasingly ask for both, meaning the promote tier opens only when the deal clears both tests. This is commercial practice that varies by investor, not a standard.

Lever four: where the fees sit

A development fee paid as a project cost is paid before the waterfall, so every partner bears it in proportion to their capital, and the developer receives it whether the deal succeeds or not. Worked example: a hypothetical 1.5 million development fee on a 50 million project, with equity of 15 million. The fee reduces the profit available to the waterfall by 1.5 million. The investor, holding 90 percent of the equity, bears about 1.35 million of that cost; the developer bears 150,000 and receives 1.5 million. The developer's net gain from the fee is 1.35 million, paid whatever happens. That is why investors examine whether fees cover real overhead or are a second, guaranteed promote.

How the best do it

Experienced institutional investors tend to apply the same principles to every developer partnership. Fees are sized to cover the developer's genuine overhead and staff, not to deliver profit. Profit comes through the promote, which is paid only on results. The developer co-invests a meaningful amount, so it shares losses as well as gains. And reporting shows every fee in dollars each quarter. A small developer can adopt all four voluntarily, and doing so is the fastest way to be trusted by better capital.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Treat fees and promote as two different assets. Fees are near-certain income, already earned when paid, and usually taxed as income. Promote is a contingent asset: until the deal is sold and the waterfall is run, its value is an estimate that can fall to zero. On your personal balance sheet, value expected promote at a conservative figure, never the pro forma figure, and record any clawback obligation as a contingent liability beside it. If most of your projected wealth is promote on one or two deals, you are more concentrated than the balance sheet looks.

Worked example: the levers interact

Levers do not simply add up; they interact, and the effect changes with the outcome. Combine a compounding preferred return with a full catch-up, using the 10 million venture from last lesson.

In the strong case, with 16 million to distribute, the full catch-up is reached either way. Once it is full, the developer receives 20 percent of all profit as promote plus 10 percent of the remaining 80 percent, which is 28 percent of the 6 million profit, or 1.68 million, whether the preferred return is simple or compounding. In that case compounding costs the developer nothing.

Now take a middling case with 13 million to distribute, so 3 million of profit.

  • Simple: the preferred return takes 2.4 million, and the remaining 0.6 million exactly fills the catch-up. The developer receives 1 plus 0.24 plus 0.6, which is 1.84 million.
  • Compounding: the preferred return takes about 2.597 million, leaving about 0.403 million for the catch-up. The developer receives 1 plus about 0.26 plus 0.403, which is about 1.663 million.

Compounding costs the developer about 177,000 dollars in the middling case and nothing in the strong case. A partner looking only at the base case would never see it. That is why every term set is modelled across a weak, base and strong case together, and why you ask your model which case each lever bites in before you trade it. Notice too that the simple-versus-compounding choice mattered most in exactly the outcome investors worry about, a deal that clears its hurdle but not by much.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing levers one at a time without seeing their combined effect, so that a compounding preferred return, a rate-only hurdle and outside fees together shift far more than intended. The control is to model every proposed term set in one waterfall spreadsheet across a weak, base and strong case before agreeing anything.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fights hard over the promote percentage and concedes compounding and fee terms in a sentence. On many deals the compounding and fee terms are worth more than a five-point change in the split.

Callback

In week 11 we learned time value of money: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later. Compounding preferred returns and internal-rate hurdles are time value written into a contract. When you see either, ask how the answer changes if the deal takes two years longer than planned.

Recap

Four levers move money between partners: simple or compounding preferred return, a catch-up, rate or multiple hurdles, and where fees sit. Model them together, size fees to overhead, and treat promote as a contingent asset.

Next: Elias on the rules: the tax character of developer fees and promote, and why the label on a dollar matters.
checklist: Calculate the preferred return both simple and compounding
Measure the dollars moved by any catch-up
Test the deal against both a rate hurdle and a multiple hurdle
Calculate the developer's net gain from fees paid as project costs
Model all proposed terms together in weak, base and strong cases
Value expected promote conservatively on your personal balance sheet
Record any clawback as a contingent liability

speak: Mr Shabazz, waterfall pricing in sixty seconds. Four levers move money between partners without changing the building. One: compounding preferred return. On 10 million at 8 percent over three years it costs about 197,000 dollars more than simple. Two: the catch-up, which lets the developer reach its full promote share of all the profit; in our example it moved 480,000 dollars to the developer. Three: hurdles. A rate hurdle rewards speed, a multiple hurdle rewards total profit, and many investors want both. Four: fees. A 1.5 million development fee paid as a project cost gives the developer a net 1.35 million whatever happens. So I model all terms together across weak, base and strong cases. And on my own balance sheet, fees are income, promote is a contingent asset valued conservatively, and any clawback is a contingent liability.
terms: Catch-up — a waterfall bucket in which the developer receives all or most distributions until it has received its agreed share of total profit.
Multiple hurdle — a threshold stated as a multiple of capital returned, such as 1.5 times, rather than as a rate of return.
Compounding preferred return — a preferred return in which unpaid amounts themselves earn a return.

hostile.q: Your development fee pays you 1.5 million before we see a dollar of profit. Why is that fair?
hostile.a: It is sized to our real cost of running the project: staff, overhead and design management over three years, and I will show you the budget behind it. It is not profit. Our profit comes only through the promote, which pays nothing unless you get your capital and preferred return first. We also co-invest alongside you, so we share any loss, and every fee appears in dollars in each quarterly report.

title: The tax character of fees and promote: why the label on a dollar matters
summary: A developer can receive money from a joint venture as a fee for services or as a share of profits. Tax systems often treat those differently in character, in timing and in indirect tax. This lesson teaches the concepts and the questions to put to an adviser, without stating any rate or rule as fact.
body:
The same dollar can arrive as a fee or as a share of profit, and many tax systems treat those two very differently. The documents, the accounts and the reality must all agree on which one it is.

Recall

Q. What is a clawback, and what makes one worth having?

A. A promise by the developer to repay promote that later proves overpaid. It is worth having only if it is backed by escrow or a guarantee from someone with assets.

Q. What is a hedge in the context of floating-rate debt?

A. A contract, such as an interest rate swap or cap, that limits the borrower's exposure to rising rates.

Q. What is a restrictive covenant on land?

A. A registered promise that limits how land may be used, such as a height or use restriction, which can bind later owners.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, your two main sources of income from a joint venture are fees and promote. Before you agree a waterfall, you need to know how each is likely to be taxed where you operate, because the after-tax value of a dollar of fee and a dollar of promote can differ materially. Everything in this lesson is conceptual. No rate, threshold, holding period or section number is stated as fact; verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: a tax adviser, chartered professional accountant or tax lawyer qualified in each relevant jurisdiction.

Character: income for services or a share of profit

In plain English, the character of income is the category tax law puts it in. A fee is usually payment for services: the developer did work and was paid for it. Many systems treat service income as ordinary business or employment-type income. A promote is usually structured as a share of the partnership's profit. Where the partnership is treated as transparent for tax, a flow-through entity in the language of week 22, the partner's share of profit may keep the character of the underlying income or gain. If the profit is a capital gain on the sale of the building, some systems allow the promote to be treated as capital in character too. Others have specific rules that treat some or all of a carried interest as income for services instead, often depending on how long the asset was held or on the nature of the partner's role.

The professional framing is this: character follows the legal substance of the arrangement, not the name in the document. A payment called promote that is really fixed compensation for work, paid whatever the result, may be treated as a fee. A fee that depends entirely on profit may look more like a share of profit. Week 24 taught substance over form; this is where it bites.

Say that out loud now.

Timing: when the tax arrives

A fee is usually taxed when it is received or earned. A share of partnership profit in a transparent entity may be taxed when the profit is allocated, which can be before any cash is distributed. That creates phantom income: tax owed on profit you have not yet received in cash. Worked example one, hypothetical: a partnership allocates 600,000 dollars of profit to the developer in a year when all cash is retained to fund a repair. If that allocation is taxable, the developer may owe tax on 600,000 while receiving nothing. Partnership agreements often address this with a tax distribution clause, which requires the venture to distribute enough cash to cover partners' tax on allocated income. Whether such a clause is needed, and how it interacts with the waterfall, is a question for your adviser.

The project side, and indirect tax

At the venture level, a development fee is usually a cost of creating the building. Many systems require such costs to be added to the building's cost base rather than deducted at once, which affects the venture's later gain on sale. A fee paid by the venture may also be subject to an indirect tax such as a value added tax or goods and services tax, which Devika would flag: whether the developer must charge it, and whether the venture can recover it, depends on the registration status of each party and the rules where the services are supplied.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A venture pays its developer a 1 million dollar development fee. Questions for the adviser, in order. Is the fee income to the developer in the year received? Must the developer charge an indirect tax on it, and if so can the venture recover that tax? Is the fee added to the building's cost base at the venture level, reducing the eventual gain? And does the developer's own structure, a company or personally, change how the fee is taxed? Four questions, four answers, all to be verified.

Matching the documents, the accounts and the reality

Cole's point from Failure Forensics applies here with force. A tax position is defended with documents. The partnership agreement must describe each payment the same way the accounts record it and the tax return reports it, and the real economics must match that description. A developer that calls a guaranteed annual payment a profit share, records it as a fee in its accounts, and reports it as a capital gain has created three descriptions of one payment and invited an auditor to choose the least favourable.

Worked example three: substance over the label

This is a composite example. A developer's agreement calls a payment of 300,000 dollars a year a "promote", but it is paid every year from the start of construction, whatever the venture earns, and it stops if the developer is replaced as manager. Read the substance: a fixed sum, paid regardless of profit, tied to continuing to provide services. That is the profile of a fee. A tax authority looking through the label may treat it that way, and the developer's planning built on the word "promote" would fall with it.

The reverse case matters as well. A payment called a fee that is paid only from profit, and only if investors clear their hurdle, has some of the profile of a profit share, and the consequences may differ again. Neither outcome is stated here as law; each depends on the jurisdiction and the facts, so verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

Sizing a tax distribution clause

Return to the 600,000 dollars of allocated profit. A tax distribution clause commonly uses an assumed rate written into the agreement, so the venture does not need each partner's private tax position. Suppose the agreement uses an assumed rate of 40 percent, a hypothetical placeholder, not an actual rate anywhere. The venture would distribute 600,000 times 0.40, which is 240,000 dollars, to cover the tax. Two drafting points follow. Is that distribution an advance against the partner's later waterfall share, so it is deducted when the waterfall is run? And does it apply to promote allocations as well as to capital? Leave either unanswered and the clause can quietly move money. The assumed rate, and whether such a clause is appropriate at all, are for your adviser.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relabelling: designing a payment to look like a share of profit for tax purposes when in substance it is a fee. Anti-avoidance rules, studied in week 24, exist precisely to look through such labels, and the penalties for an unsupported position can exceed the tax saved. The control is to design the economics first, take written advice on the character that follows, and make the documents, accounts and returns say the same thing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes promote is automatically taxed more favourably than fees and pushes everything into the promote. Character depends on the jurisdiction, on how long the asset is held and on the substance of the arrangement, and in some systems the expected advantage simply does not exist. Ask before you negotiate, not after.

Callback

In week 22 we learned that flow-through entities pass their income to their owners for tax. That is why promote can carry the character of the building's gain, and also why phantom income arises. The same feature that can help on character can hurt on timing.

Recap

Fees and promote can differ in character, in timing and in indirect tax. Character follows substance, timing can create tax before cash, and the documents, accounts and returns must agree. Every point here is conceptual; verify it against the primary source and get written advice.

Next: JAX with the numbers: reverse engineering a waterfall from what the developer was paid.
checklist: List every payment to the developer as either a fee or a share of profit
Take written advice on the likely character of each
Ask whether allocated profit can be taxed before cash is distributed
Decide whether the agreement needs a tax distribution clause
Ask whether fees attract an indirect tax and who can recover it
Confirm how development fees affect the venture's cost base
Check the agreement, the accounts and the returns describe each payment identically
Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each relevant jurisdiction
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the tax character of fees and promote in sixty seconds. A fee is usually payment for services and is often taxed as ordinary income when received. A promote is usually a share of partnership profit, and where the partnership is a flow-through, it may keep the character of the underlying gain, though some systems have specific rules that treat carried interest as service income. Character follows substance, not labels. Timing matters too: a share of profit can be taxed when allocated, before cash arrives, which is phantom income, so agreements often include a tax distribution clause. Fees may also attract indirect tax and usually add to the building's cost base. None of this is stated as fact for any country; I verify against the primary source and take written advice. And I make sure the agreement, the accounts and the tax return all describe each payment the same way.
terms: Character of income — the category, such as business income or capital gain, into which tax law places a receipt.
Phantom income — taxable income allocated to a partner before any corresponding cash is distributed.
Tax distribution clause — a partnership provision requiring cash distributions sufficient to cover partners' tax on allocated income.

hostile.q: Your promote is a fixed 400,000 dollars a year whatever happens. Why do you report it as a share of profit?
hostile.a: You are right to challenge that, and I would not. A payment that does not depend on results is in substance compensation for services, and I would expect it to be treated that way. We restructured it: a fee sized to our overhead, reported as a fee, and a promote that depends entirely on the waterfall. The agreement, our accounts and our returns describe each one the same way, and we have written advice on both.

title: Reverse engineering a waterfall: from what was paid back to what was sold
summary: Starting from the amount the developer finally received, this worked calculation runs a waterfall backwards to find the profit, the distributable cash and the sale price. It then answers a second question in reverse: what sale price does the investor need to reach its target multiple?
body:
If you know the waterfall and one partner's payout, you can work backwards to the sale price. Doing that is the fastest way to check an investor report, a promote claim or a pitch.

Recall

Q. What is the first bucket of a typical waterfall?

A. Return of capital: every partner gets back what it contributed before any return or profit is shared.

Q. What is the binding constraint when sizing a loan?

A. The test, out of coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value or loan-to-cost, that produces the smallest loan; that test decides the loan amount.

Q. What does a title search reveal before closing?

A. The registered owner and every registered interest affecting the land, such as mortgages, easements, covenants and liens.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we work backwards. In real life you will often know an outcome and not the inputs: a partner says it received 3.8 million, or an investor wants a target multiple. Reverse engineering turns those statements into a sale price you can test against the market.

The waterfall we are using

Hypothetical joint venture. Equity 10 million: investor 9 million, developer 1 million. Three-year hold. Buckets:

  1. Return of capital, pro rata.
  2. Preferred return, 8 percent simple per year, pro rata: 8 percent times 10 million times 3 years equals 2.4 million.
  3. Catch-up: 100 percent to the developer as promote until promote equals 20 percent of all profit distributed in buckets 2 and 3.
  4. Split: 80 percent to all partners pro rata, 20 percent to the developer as promote.

The percentages are hypothetical commercial terms, not standards.

Step 1: Size the catch-up

The catch-up must bring promote to 20 percent of profit, so promote equals one quarter of the preferred return already paid, because 20 divided by 80 is 0.25. That is 0.25 times 2.4 million, which equals 0.6 million. So the catch-up bucket holds 0.6 million, and it is full once total profit reaches 2.4 plus 0.6, which is 3.0 million.

Step 2: Write the developer's total as a formula

Let P be total profit, meaning distributions above returned capital, in millions. Once P is at least 3.0 million, the developer's promote is exactly 20 percent of P, which is 0.2 times P. The remaining 80 percent of P is shared pro rata, and the developer's 10 percent of that is 0.1 times 0.8 times P, which is 0.08 times P. Add its returned capital of 1 million. So the developer's total receipts equal 1 plus 0.28 times P.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: Solve for profit

The developer reports receiving 3.8 million in total. Set 1 plus 0.28 P equal to 3.8. Subtract 1: 0.28 P equals 2.8. Divide by 0.28: P equals 10 million. Check that P is at least 3.0, which it is, so the formula applies.

Step 4: Check forward

Always verify a reverse calculation by running it forward. Distributable cash equals capital plus profit: 10 plus 10 equals 20 million. Capital back: investor 9, developer 1. Preferred return 2.4: investor 2.16, developer 0.24. Catch-up 0.6 to the developer. Remaining 7.0: promote 20 percent is 1.4 to the developer; 80 percent is 5.6, shared investor 5.04 and developer 0.56. Developer total: 1 plus 0.24 plus 0.6 plus 1.4 plus 0.56 equals 3.8 million. Investor total: 9 plus 2.16 plus 5.04 equals 16.2 million. Together: 20 million. Total promote, 0.6 plus 1.4, equals 2.0 million, exactly 20 percent of the 10 million profit. The forward run confirms the answer.

Step 5: From distributions to sale price

Distributable cash is what is left after the loan and selling costs. Suppose the loan balance at sale was 20 million and selling costs, such as brokerage and legal, are a hypothetical 2 percent of the gross price. Net proceeds needed: 20 million to the partners plus 20 million to the lender, which is 40 million. Gross price equals 40 divided by 0.98, which equals about 40.8 million dollars. So a developer payout of 3.8 million implies a gross sale price of about 40.8 million. If comparable buildings would not sell for that, the payout figure is wrong.

Worked example two: the investor's target

An investor tells you it wants 1.6 times its capital. What sale price does that require? The investor's profit, once P is at least 3.0, is its 90 percent of the 80 percent pro rata share of all profit: 0.9 times 0.8 times P, which is 0.72 P. A 1.6 times multiple on 9 million is 14.4 million back, a profit of 5.4 million. So 0.72 P equals 5.4, and P equals 7.5 million. Distributable cash: 10 plus 7.5 equals 17.5 million. Add the 20 million loan: 37.5 million net. Gross price: 37.5 divided by 0.98, which equals about 38.27 million dollars. Now you can say, precisely, what the market must deliver for the investor to be satisfied.

Step 6: Units and sense checks

Keep everything in millions of dollars. Check that the catch-up formula only applies above its threshold; below 3.0 million of profit, the developer's total is different, and the formula would overstate it. And compare the implied price with a value from the income approach, the stabilised income divided by a market capitalisation rate, before believing either.

Worked example three: a payout inside the catch-up

Now the developer reports receiving 1.5 million. Try the formula first: 1 plus 0.28 P equals 1.5 gives P of about 1.786 million. Check the threshold: 1.786 is below 3.0, so the formula does not apply, and the answer is wrong.

Find the right region. With P exactly 2.4 million, the preferred return is fully paid and the catch-up has not started, so the developer has 1 plus 0.24, which is 1.24 million. With P at 3.0 million, the catch-up is full and the developer has 1.84 million. A payout of 1.5 million sits between them, so we are inside the catch-up, where every dollar of profit above 2.4 million goes to the developer.

  1. Set 1.24 plus (P minus 2.4) equal to 1.5. So P minus 2.4 equals 0.26, and P equals 2.66 million.
  2. Check forward: distributable cash is 12.66 million. Capital back, 9 and 1. Preferred return 2.4, split 2.16 and 0.24. Catch-up 0.26 to the developer. Developer total: 1 plus 0.24 plus 0.26 equals 1.5 million. Investor: 11.16 million. Together, 12.66. It holds.
  3. Gross price: 12.66 plus the 20 million loan is 32.66 million net, divided by 0.98, which is about 33.33 million.

The wrong formula would have implied distributable cash of about 11.79 million and a gross price of about 32.43 million, roughly 0.9 million too low. That is the biggest risk below, in numbers: a correct formula used outside its range gives a confident, wrong price. The habit that prevents it is to write down, before solving, which bucket the last dollar of profit fell into. Name the region first, then pick the formula for that region, then solve, then run it forward. Four steps, every time, even when the answer looks obvious.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is using a formula outside the range where it holds, for example applying the full catch-up result to a deal whose profit never filled the catch-up. The control is to check the threshold first and to always run the answer forward through every bucket.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets the lender and the selling costs, and treats distributable cash as the sale price. The partners only share what is left after both.

Callback

In week 17 we reverse engineered deals from public information: an implied land price from a known rent and return. This is the same skill applied to the equity: from a known payout or target back to the price the building must fetch.

Recap

Size the catch-up, write each partner's total as a formula above the catch-up threshold, solve, run it forward, then add the loan and selling costs to reach the gross price. A 3.8 million developer payout implied about 40.8 million; a 1.6 times investor target needed about 38.27 million.

Next: JAX in the room: presenting a waterfall to a prospective partner, and the lines that build or destroy trust.
checklist: Write out every bucket and its percentages
Calculate the catch-up amount and the profit threshold where it fills
Express the partner's total receipts as a formula above the threshold
Solve for profit and confirm it is above the threshold
Run the answer forward through every bucket
Add loan payoff and selling costs to reach the gross price
Compare the implied price with an income approach value
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, reverse engineering a waterfall in sixty seconds. Take a hypothetical 10 million dollar venture, 90 percent investor, 10 percent developer, a three-year 8 percent simple preferred return of 2.4 million, a full catch-up to 20 percent of profit, then an 80 to 20 split. The catch-up holds a quarter of the preferred return, 0.6 million, and fills at 3 million of profit. Above that, the developer receives its 1 million back plus 0.28 times profit. If it was paid 3.8 million, profit was 10 million, so 20 million was distributed. Add a 20 million loan and 2 percent selling costs and the building sold for about 40.8 million. For an investor wanting 1.6 times, its profit is 0.72 times total profit, so profit must be 7.5 million and the gross price about 38.27 million. Always run the answer forward to check it.
terms: Distributable cash — the money left for the partners after repaying debt, paying costs and funding required reserves.
Catch-up threshold — the level of total profit at which the developer's catch-up bucket is full.
Gross sale price — the price before selling costs and loan repayment are deducted.

hostile.q: You say you earned 3.8 million on this deal. What did the building actually sell for?
hostile.a: About 40.8 million gross. Under the waterfall, my 3.8 million means total profit of 10 million above the 10 million of capital, so 20 million was distributed. The loan payoff was 20 million and selling costs about 2 percent. I can run it forward bucket by bucket for you, and the sale price is in the closing statement.

title: In the room: walking a partner through your waterfall
summary: A hypothetical meeting with a sophisticated equity partner who is reviewing a joint venture term sheet already exchanged. What to say, what never to say, the question behind the question, and how to hold steady when your fees are challenged.
body:
An equity partner is not judging your percentages; it is judging whether you will be honest with its money when the deal goes wrong. Every answer about the waterfall is really an answer about that.

Recall

Q. In the reverse-engineered waterfall, what gross sale price did a 3.8 million developer payout imply?

A. About 40.8 million, after adding the 20 million loan payoff and 2 percent selling costs to the 20 million distributed.

Q. What is an interest rate cap?

A. A contract that pays the borrower when a floating reference rate rises above an agreed level, limiting the borrower's interest cost.

Q. What is a survey's role in title due diligence?

A. It shows the boundaries, improvements and any encroachments or easements on the ground, which a title search alone cannot reveal.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the scene below is hypothetical. It is a negotiation with a party that already has your term sheet, not a script for approaching investors; raising capital from the public or from individuals is governed by securities rules we study in weeks 70 and 71. Here the skill is the conversation itself: explaining a waterfall so clearly that the other side trusts the numbers and the person.

The scene

A hypothetical family office, represented by its chief investment officer and an analyst, is reviewing your term sheet for a 25 million dollar equity joint venture on a rental project. They will fund 90 percent. The analyst has built your waterfall in a spreadsheet and found that your fees total more than your co-investment. The chief investment officer opens: "Walk us through how you get paid. All of it."

The lines to say

"Gladly. There are two kinds of payment. Fees, which cover our cost of running the project, and promote, which we earn only if you do well. Let me show you both, in dollars, in a weak case and a strong case."

"Our total fees over the life of the deal are 1.9 million in the base case. Here is the overhead budget they fund: two staff, design management and reporting. We earn no profit on them."

"Our promote is tested against the whole deal to date. If you do not receive your capital and an 8 percent return, we receive no promote, and anything paid early sits half in escrow until the end."

"Here is the weak case. In it, you get your capital back and part of your preferred return, and we receive our fees and no promote. That is the case I would ask you to judge us on."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

"Our fees are market." Market is not a reason, and it signals you have not thought about whether yours are justified.

"Don't worry about the weak case, it won't happen." The partner's job is to worry about it, and dismissing it tells them you will hide bad news.

"The promote is just how it's done." It invites the reply that, in that case, they will do it differently.

The question behind the question

"Walk us through how you get paid. All of it." The real question is: "Are you paid more for doing deals than for doing them well?" Answer it directly: "We are paid enough in fees to stay in business and nothing more. Everything above that depends on your result."

When the analyst asks "Why is the catch-up full rather than partial?", the real question is "How much did you move to yourself with that one word?" Answer with the number: "In the base case the full catch-up moves about 400,000 dollars to us compared with no catch-up. In exchange, we raised our co-investment from 5 to 10 percent."

Worked example: a trade in the room

The chief investment officer asks for a compounding preferred return instead of simple. You know from your model that on a three-year base case at 8 percent, compounding costs you, through a smaller promote, roughly 200,000 dollars per 10 million of equity, about 500,000 on 25 million. Do not refuse and do not accept. Say: "Compounding is worth about half a million to you in our base case. I can accept it if we add a multiple hurdle alongside the rate hurdle, so we are both paid on total profit, not just speed." You have priced the request and traded it, rather than conceding it.

When to stay silent

After you show the weak case, stop. Let them read it. People trust what they find for themselves far more than what they are told, and silence gives them room to find it.

Holding your state

When the analyst says "Your fees exceed your investment," the instinct is to defend. Instead, slow your breathing, agree with the fact, and explain it: "That is correct, and it is why we show it on one page. The fees fund real costs; here they are. If you want, we can convert part of the development fee into additional co-investment." Agreement with a true fact lowers the temperature instantly.

Ethics: the money you hold for others

This month's thread is ethics. A waterfall gives the developer two powers: to decide when cash is distributed and to calculate who gets what. Both can be abused quietly, by timing a refinance to unlock promote or by classifying a cost to favour yourself. The standard to hold is simple: never make a decision about other people's money that you would not be willing to explain to them in writing, in advance.

A practical form of that standard is a written distribution policy: who decides, on what test, with what notice to the partner, and who checks the waterfall calculation. When the calculation is checked by someone who is not paid the promote, both sides can trust the answer. Write that policy before you need it.

The second hard question: the refinance

Later in the meeting the chief investment officer asks: "If rents come in strong, will you refinance in year three and take promote early?" The question behind the question is the composite case from Ford's lesson: will cash leave before the result is known?

Say: "We can refinance, but it does not unlock promote by itself. Promote is tested on the whole deal to date, so refinance proceeds first return your capital. If an interim promote were ever paid, half stays in escrow until the sale, and we guarantee the rest." Then put a number on it. Worked example, hypothetical: if an interim promote of 800,000 dollars were paid, 400,000 would sit in escrow and the other 400,000 would rest on the principals' guarantee. Show it on the page, beside the refinance case in your model.

Never say: "We would never refinance." You might, for good reasons, and a promise you cannot keep costs more trust than the question was worth.

The question you ask them

A good meeting runs both ways. Before it ends, ask: "Who on your side approves distributions and checks the waterfall each quarter, and how quickly can you respond to a capital call?" A partner that cannot fund a call on time is a risk to your schedule, and the answer tells you how the relationship will run when something goes wrong.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defending your fees instead of explaining them, which makes a reasonable term look like something hidden. The control is one page showing every fee and the promote, in dollars, in a weak and a strong case, handed over before the partner asks.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leads with the strong case. Lead with the weak case; it is the one that earns trust.

Callback

In week 3 we studied incentives and trust. A partner will forgive a bad outcome far sooner than a surprise. Showing your full compensation in a weak case is the deliberate removal of surprise.

Recap

Show both kinds of payment, in dollars, in a weak case first. Price every request before trading it. Agree with true facts, then explain them. Never use "market" as a reason.

Next: Kema reviews the week: six questions, a Red Pen drill on a waterfall clause, and the two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: Prepare one page of every fee and the promote in dollars
Show the weak case before the strong case
Price every likely partner request in dollars before the meeting
Bring the overhead budget that justifies the fees
Explain the clawback escrow and the deal-to-date test
Write a distribution policy naming who decides and who checks
After showing the weak case, stop and let them read
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the waterfall room in sixty seconds. The partner asks how I get paid, all of it. The real question is whether I am paid more for doing deals than for doing them well. So I show two kinds of payment, fees and promote, in dollars, and I lead with the weak case: in it they get their capital back and part of their return, and I get fees and no promote. Fees fund real overhead; here is the budget. Promote is tested deal to date, and half of anything paid early sits in escrow. When they ask for a compounding preferred return, I price it, about half a million in the base case, and trade it for a multiple hurdle. I never say our fees are market, never dismiss the weak case. And I keep a written distribution policy, because deciding about other people's money is an ethical duty, not just a clause.
terms: Distribution policy — a written rule stating who decides distributions, on what test, with what notice, and who checks the calculation.
Co-investment — the developer's own capital contributed alongside its investors, sharing in losses as well as gains.
Weak case — a deliberately unfavourable scenario used to show how each party fares if the deal underperforms.

hostile.q: Your fees exceed your co-investment. Why should we believe your interests are aligned with ours?
hostile.a: Because the fees only cover cost, and here is the budget showing that, while every dollar of profit we earn depends on your result. In the weak case you get your capital back and we earn no promote. If you prefer more alignment, we will convert part of the development fee into additional co-investment, so more of our money sits beside yours.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 38 review: waterfalls, promote and fees
summary: Six questions on waterfalls, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical waterfall clause with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week you learned to read a waterfall as an order, to price each lever in it, and to see that the most dangerous terms are about timing and security, not percentages.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a rate hurdle and a multiple hurdle?

A. A rate hurdle is an internal rate of return and rewards speed; a multiple hurdle is a multiple of capital returned and rewards total profit.

Q. What does a lender mean by sizing to debt yield?

A. Setting the loan so that net operating income divided by the loan meets the lender's minimum percentage, whatever the interest rate.

Q. Why does a buyer read a condominium declaration before buying a unit?

A. Because it defines what the unit is, the share of common elements and expenses, and the rules that will bind the owner.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, answer each question aloud before reading the answer. If you hesitate, reread that day's lesson.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the typical buckets of a waterfall, in order? Answer: Return of capital, preferred return, sometimes a catch-up, then a split of the remaining profit that includes the developer's promote.

Question 2. Why should a promote pay nothing in a weak case? Answer: Because it rewards performance. If investors have not received their capital and preferred return, a promote would transfer money to the developer rather than share upside.

Question 3. What made the composite clawback worthless? Answer: It was given by a holding company with no assets, with no escrow and no personal guarantee, and promote had already left the venture.

Question 4. What does a full catch-up do? Answer: It lets the developer receive all, or most, of the dollars after the preferred return until its promote equals its agreed share of all the profit, not just profit above the preferred return.

Question 5. What is phantom income? Answer: Taxable profit allocated to a partner before any cash is distributed, which is why agreements often include a tax distribution clause. Verify the treatment against the primary source.

Question 6. What was Rule 38? Answer: No promote is paid until investors have their capital and preferred return on the whole deal to date, and every clawback is backed by escrow or a guarantee from someone with assets.

Say that out loud now.

Week recap

Day 1 built the waterfall and showed a good and a weak outcome. Day 2 took apart a composite collapse caused by early promote and an unsecured clawback. Day 3 priced four levers: compounding, catch-up, hurdles and fees. Day 4 separated fees from promote by character, timing and indirect tax, as concepts to verify. Day 5 worked a waterfall backwards to a sale price. Day 6 explained the waterfall to a partner, weak case first.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical waterfall clause and find the defects before reading on.

Distributable Cash shall be paid: first, to the Partners pro rata until each has received its Capital; second, to the Partners pro rata until each has received a Preferred Return of 8 percent; third, 100 percent to the Developer until caught up; fourth, 80 percent to the Partners pro rata and 20 percent to the Developer. Each Distribution shall be calculated separately. The Developer shall return any excess Promote upon request. Fees shall be as agreed from time to time.

The defects. First, the preferred return does not say per year, simple or compounding, so 8 percent could mean 8 percent in total. Second, "until caught up" does not say caught up to what share of which profit. Third, each distribution calculated separately is the defect from day two: promote can be paid on a refinance and never tested against the final result. Fourth, the clawback says "upon request", with no timing, no escrow and no guarantor, so it is a hope rather than a protection. Fifth, "fees as agreed from time to time" lets fees change later without a cap or a schedule; fees must be listed in dollars or by formula, with a total. A sixth, subtler one: Capital is not defined, so it is unclear whether returned capital from a refinance reduces it.

Boardroom drill

Explain the week to a board in two minutes, aloud, then compare.

Model answer: "Our joint venture pays out cash in a fixed order. Partners get their capital back, then an 8 percent simple annual preferred return, then we get a catch-up to 20 percent of profit, and the rest splits 80 to 20. In a weak case we earn fees, which only cover our overhead, and no promote. In the base case our share of profit is about 28 percent on a 10 percent co-investment. Promote is tested against the whole deal to date, half of anything paid early is escrowed, and the principals guarantee the clawback. Fees are listed in dollars, total 1.9 million, and are reported quarterly. On tax, our fees and our promote may be treated differently; we have written advice on each, and our documents, accounts and returns describe every payment the same way."

What the board will ask next

Expect three follow-ups. "What happens if the hold is two years longer?" Answer with the effect on the preferred return and the promote. "Who checks the waterfall calculation?" Name someone who is not paid the promote. "What is your personal exposure?" Name the clawback guarantee and its cap.

Score yourself

Record your answer and score it 1 to 5 for accuracy, structure, composure and whether you handled the hard question about fees. Repeat until each score is at least 4.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is money leaving the venture before the result is known. The control is deal-to-date testing, a secured clawback and fees on one page.

One more calculation to carry

Before the boardroom drill, check where the model answer's figure of about 28 percent comes from, because it is easy to say 21 by mistake. The 21 percent came from day one, with no catch-up: 1.248 million of a 6 million profit, about 20.8 percent. Now add the full catch-up from day three. Once the catch-up is full, the developer receives 20 percent of all profit as promote plus 10 percent of the remaining 80 percent, which is 28 percent. On the same 6 million profit that is 1.68 million, about 432,000 dollars more than without the catch-up. The model answer mentions a catch-up, so its percentage must be 28, not 21. Saying the wrong one to a board, even by accident, is exactly the kind of surprise that costs trust.

Then run the weak case aloud as well: 12 million to distribute, capital back, 2 million of the 2.4 million preferred return, and no promote. If you can say both cases from memory, you understand the waterfall. If you cannot, the gap is almost always in the catch-up, so rerun day five's forward check by hand until the buckets add back to the cash distributed.

Practising this week

Take one real or sample joint venture agreement and read only its definitions of capital, preferred return and distributable cash. Write in one sentence what each means. Then find where fees are listed and add them up in dollars. Twenty minutes, once, teaches more than a second reading of this lesson. Finally, write one line that answers the board's third follow-up for you personally: if you were the developer, what clawback guarantee would you sign, and how much of your own balance sheet would stand behind it? Keep the answer, and revisit it when week 70 reaches securities and investor protection.

The beginner's mistake

Negotiating the split and ignoring the definitions. The definitions decide the money.

Callback

In week 37 the capital stack decided what reaches the common equity. The waterfall decides how that common equity's share is divided. Always run them together: the stack first, then the waterfall on what is left.

Recap

Order, pricing, timing, character and trust: those were the five ideas of the week. Read definitions first, model every term together, and lead with the weak case.

head: The six questions
speak: Mr Shabazz, week 38 in sixty seconds. A waterfall pays cash in order: capital back, preferred return, sometimes a catch-up, then a split that includes the developer's promote. The promote should pay nothing when investors do badly. The composite case failed because promote left on a refinance and the clawback was given by an empty company, so Rule 38 says no promote until capital and preferred return are covered on the whole deal to date, with a clawback backed by escrow or a guarantee. Four levers move money without changing the building: compounding, catch-up, rate or multiple hurdles, and where fees sit. Fees and promote can differ in tax character and timing, including phantom income, so take written advice and keep every document consistent. Working backwards, a payout implies a sale price. And in the room, lead with the weak case.
terms: Distribution waterfall — the ordered rules for paying a venture's distributable cash to its partners.
Promote — the developer's share of profit above its share of capital, earned on performance.
Clawback — the developer's obligation to repay promote later shown to have been overpaid.

hostile.q: Your clause says each distribution is calculated separately. What stops you taking promote on a refinance and leaving us short?
hostile.a: As drafted, nothing, and that is a defect. We will change it to a deal-to-date calculation, so promote is paid only once your capital and preferred return are covered on everything distributed so far, escrow half of any promote paid before sale, and have the principals guarantee the clawback.
